subject.title: Berkeley — Measure X (Rent Ordinance Amendment Measure)

text: Shall the measure to amend the Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance by making most rent control and registration exemptions inapplicable to units that were not exempt when the current tenancy began; allowing modification or waiver of fees for subsidized units owned or leased by nonprofits; changing the annual registration deadline; limiting annual rent increases to ten percent; and allowing tenant associations in smaller properties, be adopted?

analysis.title: Impartial Analysis
analysis.by: Farimah Faiz Brown, Berkeley City Attorney

text:
This measure was placed on the ballot by the City Council of the City of Berkeley.
If approved, the measure would amend the Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance (the “Ordinance”) by: 1. Providing that certain exemptions from rent control and just-cause eviction, including the exemptions for certain Accessory Dwelling Units and certain owner-occupied duplexes, would apply only if the unit was exempt when the current tenancy began. If the measure is approved, a tenant who first moved into a unit that was not exempt would be covered under the Ordinance even if the unit would otherwise qualify for an exemption at a later date during the tenancy.
2. Prohibiting property owners from raising the lawful periodic rent by more than 10% in a one-year period.
3. Allowing the Rent Stabilization Board (the “Board”) to adopt regulations to waive or reduce fees for government-subsidized rental units owned, leased or controlled by nonprofit organizations. 4. Allowing, to the extent permitted by state and local law, owners of single-family homes or new construction buildings to voluntarily agree to have their properties subject to the Ordinance in exchange for financial assistance.
5. Lowering from ten to five the number of rental units on a property for the tenants who live at that property to be eligible to form a tenant association. This change would apply to properties that are not managed by a property management company. 6. Providing that, once established, a tenant association in a property managed by a property management company remains authorized under the Ordinance even if the company later ceases to manage the rental units.
7. Clarifying that a property owner’s failure to confer in good faith with a tenant association may support a petition for a rent reduction.

8. Removing the requirement for owners of partially covered rental units to re-register units with the Board within fifteen days of the commencement of a new tenancy.
9. Making certain administrative changes, including providing for paperless billing, clarifying the process for depositing and distributing relocation assistance payments during owner move-in evictions, and changing the annual registration fee deadline from July 1 to September 30 of each year. The measure would also make various non-substantive changes such as improving readability, removing outdated language and fixing typographical errors.
The measure will be adopted if approved by a simple majority of voters.

strong: Vote YES on Measure X

text:
, placed on the ballot by unanimous vote of the City Council to make common-sense tweaks to the Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance.
Measure X will:
Enable the Rent Board to waive fees for non-profit affordable housing providers.
Align Berkeley with state law by setting an overall maximum 10% cap on annual rent increases.
Ensure that tenants who begin their tenancy with protections are not stripped of their protections arbitrarily, while still allowing small landlords to access exemptions for future tenancies.
Enable, but not require, the City Council to enact programs to create new rent-controlled housing stock.
Close loopholes used by corporate landlords to undermine tenant unions.

Make administrative changes to the Ordinance to increase efficiency.
Measure X was crafted through a collaborative process between the Rent Board, the City Council, tenant advocates, non-profit affordable housing providers, and small landlords to ensure a final product that was acceptable to all parties. Measure X represents the first time in over a decade that a measure to amend the Rent Stabilization Ordinance passed Council

strong: unanimously

text:
.
Passing Measure X will reduce financial burdens on non-profit affordable housing organizations who provide key services to low income and elderly Berkeley residents, all while maintaining existing legal protections for vulnerable residents. It will also enable the Rent Board to provide more efficient and effective services to landlords and tenants alike by modernizing and streamlining administrative processes. Measure X is endorsed by:
Berkeley Tenants Union
East Bay Housing Organizations
Berkeley-based non-profit affordable housing organizations including Resources for Community Development, Satellite Affordable Housing Associates, and Bay Area Community Land Trust
Vote Yes on Measure X, Common Sense Changes to the Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance. Learn more at YesOnXBerkeley.org.

arguments.disclaimer: Arguments in support of or in opposition to the proposed laws are the opinions of the authors.

strong: Measure X is a hodgepodge of policy change, and its
consequences are clear.
First, Measure X makes an important admission

text: -by carving out nonprofits, it acknowledges what City Hall avoids saying: Berkeley’s ever-increasing fees and regulations raise the cost of providing rental housing—ultimately putting upward pressure on rents for everyone.

strong: Second, Measure X further chills middle-income
housing.

text: Homeowners considering an Accessory Dwelling Unit, duplex, or lot split need clear and predictable rules. Instead, Measure X

changes regulations intended to protect homeowners who live alongside their tenants. Every change adds uncertainty, expense, and risk. Berkeley’s middle-income housing opportunities are dying by a thousand cuts.

strong: Third, Measure X spotlights the Rent Board’s
inefficiency.

text: With an $8 million budget funded largely by rental housing fees—and nearly 70% of it devoted to staffing alone—the Rent Board still doesn’t deliver meaningful results for tenants. Instead, tenants get another ballot measure reshuffling fees and regulations, while doing little to prevent tenant displacement.

strong: Real solutions, such as emergency rental assistance,
would do far more to keep struggling tenants housed
than Measure X ever will.

text: Measure X is costly, complicated, and emblematic of a Rent Board more focused on bureaucracy than delivering practical solutions.

strong: Vote NO on Measure X.

strong: Berkeley has a housing affordability problem. Measure
X does nothing to solve it.

text: Let’s be real. Measure X adds costs, complexity and legal risk—but does little to help tenants who are struggling to pay the rent.

strong: Measure X
does not

text: Create affordable housing
Provide rental assistance to families struggling to pay rent
Make housing more affordable for Berkeley renters

strong: Measure X
does:

text: Impose stringent rules on small property owners who live next to their tenants
Exempt fees for management companies already getting tax breaks

Make rental housing too risky for small property owners
Berkeley voters already made sweeping changes to rental housing laws just two years ago—now city government wants to change the rules again.

strong: The Berkeley Rent Board’s budget is over $8
million annually.

text: A large share of that money goes towards inflated bureaucratic salaries. Tenants need more of those resources directed toward what’s proven to actually keep people housed: emergency rental assistance and eviction prevention.

strong: Berkeley needs more housing, not more barriers.

text: We should be encouraging homeowners to create and provide more rental housing—not make it harder and more expensive.

strong: Exempting Rent Board fees for non-profits only
makes housing more expensive for everyone else.

text: Waiving fees for some landlords doesn’t lower the rent for tenants, it just shifts the burden of higher rents to tenants in for-profit housing.

strong: Measure X creates more uncertainty for small property
owners.

text: New rules create confusion and legal risk for those thinking about building or renting out their home’s Accessory Dwelling Unit.

strong: Measure X creates more paperwork, penalties and
lawsuits, costing taxpayers and citizens more money.

text: Increased risk and liability translate to higher starting rents, deferred building improvements, and fewer people willing to provide rental housing.

strong: Tenants need real help—not more layers of bureaucracy.
Vote NO on Measure X

text:
This is an inaccurate and bad-faith argument against Measure X, written by for-profit landlord and realtor lobbyists.
Measure X doesn’t need to create a rental assistance program; Berkeley

strong: already has one

text:
that has protected thousands of people from displacement. Measure X contains minor, common-sense refinements to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance that ensure it works for everyone.
When these lobbyists write “management companies already getting tax breaks,”

strong: they actually mean nonprofit
affordable housing providers

text: serving Berkeley’s lowest-income households. Measure X doesn’t automatically exempt them from fees; it allows the Rent Board to reduce their fees based on an objective analysis of the services they already deliver to their tenants. This is one way the City can support affordable housing and keep our neighbors housed. Measure X is a thoughtfully-negotiated compromise between the Rent Board, tenant advocates, nonprofit affordable housing providers, and small landlords and placed on the ballot by a unanimous vote of the City Council. In fact, the Berkeley Property Owners Association (BPOA),

strong: was consulted repeatedly during its drafting

text: and committed

strong: in writing

text: to not opposing Measure X in exchange for multiple substantive changes that are included in the text of the measure. It’s disappointing to see BPOA now misrepresent the very measure that it helped shape. Voters deserve facts, not scare tactics. When you read Measure X, you will find a reasonable, targeted, and carefully-negotiated proposal that strengthens the administration of the Rent Stabilization Ordinance, supports housing stability, and keeps people in their homes and off the streets.
